title: Methocarbamol and Alcohol: Risks, Timing, and Warning Signs
excerpt: Can you drink on methocarbamol (Robaxin)? Why the muscle relaxant and alcohol stack sedation, how long to wait after your last dose, and the warning signs that need help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on methocarbamol (Robaxin)? Why it and alcohol stack sedation, how long to wait after your last dose, and warning signs that need help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** methocarbamol (brand name Robaxin) and alcohol should not be mixed. Methocarbamol works by quieting your central nervous system, and alcohol does the same thing. Taken together, they stack drowsiness, dizziness, blurred vision, and slowed reactions, and they can leave you far more impaired than either would alone. The prescribing information for methocarbamol tells doctors to caution patients about combining it with alcohol and other central nervous system depressants for exactly this reason. This guide explains what's actually happening in your body, how methocarbamol differs from other muscle relaxants, how long to wait after your last dose, and the warning signs that mean you should get help.

**The quick rules:** The safest plan is to skip alcohol while you're taking methocarbamol. Most courses are short, often a week or two, so it's usually a brief ask. If you've already been drinking, don't take a dose on top of it to help you sleep, don't drive, and don't add other sleepy medicines such as Benadryl, sleep aids, opioid painkillers, benzodiazepines, or gabapentin. If someone who mixed methocarbamol and alcohol is very hard to wake, confused, fainting, having a seizure, or breathing slowly, call 911.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and the exact medicines you take. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking** if you've been prescribed methocarbamol, especially if you also take opioids, benzodiazepines, sleep medicines, gabapentin, antihistamines, or antidepressants, or if you're over 65, pregnant, or have liver or kidney problems or myasthenia gravis. **Call 911 or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US)** if someone who mixed methocarbamol and alcohol is hard to wake, confused, very dizzy or fainting, has a seizure, or is breathing slowly or shallowly.

## What Methocarbamol Is and How It Works

Methocarbamol is a prescription muscle relaxant. Doctors use it alongside rest and physical therapy for short-term relief of painful muscle spasms, such as a pulled back, a stiff neck, or a strain from lifting or sport. It has been around since the 1950s and is one of the more commonly prescribed muscle relaxants in the United States.

You'll see it under a few names:

- **Robaxin** is the best-known brand. You'll also see **Robaxin-750**, which simply refers to the 750 mg tablet strength.
- **Generic methocarbamol** comes as 500 mg and 750 mg tablets, usually taken several times a day.
- **Injectable methocarbamol** is used in hospitals and occasionally for tetanus-related muscle spasms.
- **Combination products** are sold in some countries. In Canada, for example, methocarbamol is available without a prescription in combinations with acetaminophen (Robaxacet) or ibuprofen (Robax Platinum). That matters for drinkers, and we cover it below.

Here's the part most people don't realize: methocarbamol doesn't work directly on your muscles. The exact way it works isn't fully understood, but its relaxing effect is thought to come from general depression of the central nervous system, meaning it slows activity in the brain and spinal cord. It doesn't relax muscle fibers themselves or block the nerve signals at the muscle. In plain terms, a meaningful part of how it "relaxes" you is by making your nervous system calmer and more sluggish.

That's also why its most common side effects are the ones you'd expect from a mild sedative:

- Drowsiness and sleepiness
- Dizziness and lightheadedness
- Blurred vision
- Headache and nausea
- Slower reactions and poorer coordination

Methocarbamol is generally considered one of the less sedating options in its class, and many people tolerate it well. But "less sedating" is not the same as "not sedating," and the drug's own labeling warns that it may impair the mental or physical abilities needed for driving or operating machinery.

One harmless but alarming side effect is worth knowing about: methocarbamol can turn your urine brown, black, blue, or green. This is a known effect of the drug and isn't a sign of harm on its own. It's worth mentioning because people who notice it after a night of drinking sometimes panic and assume something is wrong with their liver or kidneys. If you notice dark urine together with yellow eyes or skin, right-sided belly pain, or feeling very unwell, though, get checked.

## Why Methocarbamol and Alcohol Don't Mix

Alcohol is also a central nervous system depressant. It slows reaction time, dulls judgment, affects balance, and makes you sleepy. When you take methocarbamol and drink, you're pressing on the same brake twice. That's the core of the interaction: not a chemical reaction in your liver, but two sedating effects landing on the same system at the same time.

### More sedation and impairment

The most common, everyday problem is that you get far more drowsy and impaired than you expect. People describe feeling heavy, foggy, wobbly on their feet, or "out of it" after one or two drinks that would normally barely register. In practice, that leads to:

- **Falls and re-injury.** Many people are on methocarbamol because they've hurt their back or neck. Stumbling while unsteady is an easy way to make an injury worse, and older adults are at the highest risk.
- **Unsafe driving.** Methocarbamol alone can blur vision and slow reactions. Add alcohol and you may be impaired well below the legal alcohol limit. A breath test won't measure the drug, but you can still be charged with impaired driving in many places.
- **Dosing mistakes.** When you're drowsy and a bit drunk, it's easy to forget you already took a dose, or to take an extra one "to help you sleep."

### Blurred vision and dizziness stack too

Methocarbamol's label lists blurred vision, dizziness, and lightheadedness among its side effects. Alcohol causes all three as well. Low blood pressure and fainting have also been reported with methocarbamol. Together, these make standing up quickly, walking stairs at night, or getting out of the bath riskier than usual.

### The "third sedative" problem

On its own, a normal dose of methocarbamol is not known for dangerously slowing breathing. The serious risk shows up when methocarbamol and alcohol are combined with a third sedating drug, such as an opioid painkiller, a benzodiazepine like Xanax or Valium, gabapentin or pregabalin, a sedating antihistamine, or a prescription sleep aid. Each one adds more depression of the brain, including the part that keeps you breathing.

This is a real concern for people with back injuries, who are sometimes given a muscle relaxant and a painkiller at the same time, occasionally by different doctors. The prescribing information for methocarbamol notes that the limited reports of methocarbamol overdose have frequently involved alcohol or other central nervous system depressants, with symptoms that include nausea, drowsiness, blurred vision, low blood pressure, seizures, and coma. If you're on more than one of these medicines, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before you drink at all. Our guides to [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol) and [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol) explain those combinations in more detail.

### Alcohol may make your back worse, not better

There's another, quieter problem. Muscle relaxants work best alongside rest, gentle movement, good sleep, and physical therapy. Alcohol disrupts deep sleep, dehydrates you, and makes the next day's stiffness and fatigue worse. Drinking can also mask pain, so you overdo it and then pay for it. Even setting the drug interaction aside, alcohol tends to work against the recovery you're taking the medicine for.

## Methocarbamol vs. Other Muscle Relaxants With Alcohol

People often search for "Robaxin vs. Flexeril" when they're trying to work out which is less risky with a drink. Here's how the common options compare. None of them is safe to mix with alcohol; the differences are in how and for how long.

| Muscle relaxant | How sedating on its own | Roughly how long it stays in your system | Extra concerns with alcohol |
|---|---|---|---|
| Methocarbamol (Robaxin) | Mild to moderate | Short half-life, about 1 to 2 hours in healthy adults per the label | Stacked sedation, dizziness, blurred vision; frequent dosing means drug is usually on board |
| Cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril, Amrix) | Moderate to high | Long half-life, often around 18 hours or more | Strong sedation, anticholinergic effects, serotonin and heart rhythm warnings |
| Tizanidine (Zanaflex) | Moderate to high | Short half-life | Alcohol can raise tizanidine levels; low blood pressure and sedation |
| Carisoprodol (Soma) | High | Converted to a longer-acting sedative | Controlled substance, misuse potential, risky with any depressant |

The short half-life of methocarbamol is the one genuine advantage it has here. It leaves the body much faster than cyclobenzaprine, so the wait after your last dose is shorter. But that doesn't make it a "drinking-friendly" muscle relaxant. While you're taking it on schedule, there's almost always some of it in your system. For a closer look at the most commonly prescribed alternative, see our guide to [cyclobenzaprine and alcohol](/never-hungover/cyclobenzaprine-and-alcohol).

## Can You Have One Drink on Methocarbamol?

This is the question most people actually want answered. The label doesn't set a "safe" number of drinks. It advises caution about combining methocarbamol with alcohol at all. There's no official amount that's considered fine.

What you can say honestly:

- **One drink will probably hit you harder than usual.** Plan as if it will. Don't drive, cycle, or do anything that needs good balance or quick reactions.
- **Your risk depends on more than the drink.** Your dose, how recently you took it, your age, your body size, whether you've eaten, and every other medicine you take all change the picture.
- **Some people should skip alcohol entirely while on it.** That includes anyone also taking an opioid, benzodiazepine, gabapentin, sleep aid, or sedating antihistamine, anyone over 65, and anyone with liver or kidney disease.

Whether any alcohol is okay for *you* is a good, quick question for your prescriber or pharmacist. They can look at your full medication list and give you a straight answer.

## How Long After Methocarbamol Can You Drink?

There's no official waiting period that applies to everyone, but the drug's half-life gives a useful guide. A half-life is how long it takes your body to clear half of a drug. The methocarbamol label lists a plasma half-life of roughly 1 to 2 hours in healthy adults. A drug is generally considered mostly cleared after about four to five half-lives.

For a typical healthy adult, that suggests most of a dose is gone within roughly 5 to 10 hours. To build in a margin, many people find it sensible to wait at least 12 hours after their last dose before having a drink, and longer if any of the following apply:

- **You're older.** The label notes that the half-life is somewhat longer in elderly people.
- **You have liver disease.** In people with cirrhosis, the label reports that methocarbamol clears much more slowly, and the half-life is prolonged.
- **You have kidney problems.** Clearance is reduced in people with kidney impairment.
- **You've been taking high doses.** Early treatment often uses larger doses several times a day, which means more drug to clear.

Two practical points:

1. **If you're still taking it on schedule, waiting a few hours doesn't help much.** Methocarbamol is usually taken three to four times a day, so the next dose arrives before the last one has cleared. The realistic options are to skip alcohol until you've finished the course, or to ask your doctor whether you can pause a dose.
2. **Working the other way, wait for the alcohol to clear before your next dose.** Your body processes roughly one standard drink per hour on average, though this varies a lot between people. After a heavy night, alcohol can still be in your blood the next morning.

If you need a precise answer for your dose and health, ask your pharmacist. This is exactly the kind of question they're trained to answer.

## Can You Take Methocarbamol After Drinking to Help You Sleep?

It's not a good idea. Taking a muscle relaxant at bedtime after drinking means both drugs peak while you're falling asleep, which is when combined sedation is most dangerous and when nobody is watching. If you've been drinking and your back is sore, it's usually safer to skip that dose. Missing one dose of a muscle relaxant is rarely a problem, and you can pick up your normal schedule once the alcohol has cleared.

If you're struggling to sleep after drinking, our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's going on and what helps without adding another sedative.

## The Hidden Painkiller Problem: Combination Products

In some countries, methocarbamol is sold in combination tablets with other pain relievers. In Canada, for example, over-the-counter products pair it with acetaminophen (Robaxacet) or ibuprofen (Robax Platinum). If you live in or travel from one of those places, read the label carefully, because both partner drugs have their own alcohol issues:

- **Acetaminophen and alcohol** can strain the liver, especially with high doses, repeated doses, or regular heavy drinking. Acetaminophen also hides in many cold, flu, and sleep products, so it's easy to double up. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) covers safe limits.
- **Ibuprofen and alcohol** together raise the risk of stomach irritation and bleeding, and both can be hard on the kidneys when you're dehydrated. Our [ibuprofen and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) covers this.

So with a combination product, you're managing two interactions at once: the sedation from methocarbamol, plus the liver or stomach risk from the painkiller. Count every source of acetaminophen or ibuprofen you take in a day.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from mixing methocarbamol and alcohol if you:

- **Take other sedating medicines**, especially opioids, benzodiazepines, gabapentin or pregabalin, sleep aids, or sedating antihistamines like diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
- **Are over 65.** The American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria advise generally avoiding skeletal muscle relaxants, including methocarbamol, in older adults because they're poorly tolerated and raise fall risk
- **Have liver or kidney disease**, which slows how quickly methocarbamol is cleared
- **Have myasthenia gravis** and take a medicine such as pyridostigmine. The label cautions that methocarbamol may weaken the effect of these drugs
- **Have a seizure disorder.** The injectable form in particular carries a seizure caution, and seizures have been reported in overdoses
- **Are pregnant or breastfeeding.** The label advises against use unless a doctor decides the benefit outweighs the risk
- **Drink heavily or binge on a regular basis**, which makes it harder to time doses and raises the chance of dangerous combinations

If any of these apply, a five-minute conversation with your pharmacist or doctor is worth it.

## When to Get Help Right Away

Most of the time, mixing a single drink with methocarbamol leads to feeling much sleepier and dizzier than expected, and a groggy next morning. That's unpleasant, but it passes. The signs below are different. They suggest dangerous central nervous system depression or an overdose.

**Call 911 or go to the emergency room if someone who mixed methocarbamol and alcohol:**

- Is very hard to wake up, or can't be woken
- Is breathing slowly, shallowly, or irregularly, or is snoring or gurgling in an unusual way
- Is confused, slurring badly, or not making sense
- Faints, or is so dizzy they can't stand
- Has a seizure
- Has bluish lips or fingertips

While you wait for help, keep the person on their side so they won't choke if they vomit, and don't leave them alone. Don't try to "sleep it off" on their behalf. You can also call **Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222** (US) for advice if you're unsure how serious things are, including if someone may have taken more methocarbamol than prescribed.

Get a non-urgent medical check if you notice yellow skin or eyes, a rash, itching, or swelling of the face or lips after taking methocarbamol, with or without alcohol. Allergic reactions are uncommon but possible.

## What About the Hangover the Next Day?

Even when nothing dangerous happens, people often say the morning after mixing methocarbamol and alcohol feels worse than a normal hangover. That makes sense. Both cause drowsiness, dizziness, and headache, and alcohol adds dehydration and poor sleep on top.

If you're there now:

- **Don't take your next dose until the alcohol has cleared.** Then resume your normal schedule. Don't double up.
- **Hydrate and eat something.** Water and a simple meal help with nausea and lightheadedness.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** If you reach for acetaminophen or ibuprofen, take a single standard dose with food and check that it isn't already in a combination product you're using.
- **Don't drive** until you feel completely clear-headed.
- **Avoid other sedating "remedies."** Night-time cold medicines and antihistamine sleep aids add more sedation. Our article on [Benadryl for a hangover](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover) explains why.

## A Note on DHM and Supplements

Some people look for a supplement that will let them drink while on medication. There isn't one. **There is no good evidence that DHM, or any supplement, reduces the interaction between methocarbamol and alcohol, and nothing makes the combination safe.** The interaction is about two sedating drugs acting on your nervous system at once, and no pill undoes that.

There's also a specific reason for caution. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is thought to act on the brain's GABA system, which many sedating drugs also affect. That's part of why it's studied for alcohol, but it also means you should check with your doctor or pharmacist before combining DHM with methocarbamol or any other sedating medicine. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers this in more depth.

Once you've finished your course of methocarbamol and you're drinking normally again, DHM is something some people add to their routine. The research is promising but early: much of it comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. If you want to try it after you're off the medication, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and the habits in our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) matter more than any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- Methocarbamol (Robaxin) and alcohol both depress the central nervous system. Together they cause much more drowsiness, dizziness, blurred vision, and impairment than either alone.
- The label advises caution about combining them and sets no safe amount of alcohol. The simplest plan is to skip drinking until your course is finished.
- Methocarbamol clears faster than many muscle relaxants, with a half-life of about 1 to 2 hours in healthy adults. Waiting at least 12 hours after your last dose is a cautious general approach, and longer if you're older or have liver or kidney problems.
- The biggest danger comes from adding a third sedating drug, such as an opioid, benzodiazepine, gabapentin, or sleep aid.
- Never drive after mixing them, and don't take a dose after drinking to help you sleep.
- Call 911 if someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, confused, fainting, or having a seizure.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking methocarbamol?**

It's best not to. Methocarbamol works by depressing the central nervous system, and alcohol does the same. The prescribing information advises caution about combining them, and together they can cause heavy drowsiness, dizziness, blurred vision, and slowed reactions. Most courses are short, so the simplest plan is to skip alcohol until you've finished. If you want to drink, ask your doctor or pharmacist first.

**Is Robaxin and alcohol the same as methocarbamol and alcohol?**

Yes. Robaxin is a brand name for methocarbamol, and Robaxin-750 refers to the 750 mg tablet. Generic methocarbamol tablets contain the same active drug and carry the same caution about alcohol and other sedating substances.

**How long after taking methocarbamol can I drink alcohol?**

The label lists a half-life of about 1 to 2 hours in healthy adults, so most of a dose is usually cleared within roughly 5 to 10 hours. Waiting at least 12 hours after your last dose is a cautious general approach. Wait longer if you're older or have liver or kidney problems, since the drug clears more slowly. If you're still taking it on schedule, the safer option is to skip alcohol until the course is finished. Your pharmacist can give you a specific answer for your dose.

**Can I have one beer on methocarbamol?**

The label doesn't set a safe number of drinks. Even one drink is likely to affect you more than usual, so don't drive or do anything that needs balance or quick reactions. If you're over 65, have liver or kidney problems, or take an opioid, benzodiazepine, gabapentin, sleep aid, or sedating antihistamine, talk to your doctor before having any alcohol.

**Is methocarbamol safer than cyclobenzaprine with alcohol?**

Neither is safe to mix with alcohol. Methocarbamol is generally considered less sedating and leaves the body much faster, with a half-life of about 1 to 2 hours versus roughly 18 hours or more for cyclobenzaprine. That means a shorter wait after your last dose. But both stack sedation with alcohol, and the risks rise sharply with other sedating medicines.

**Can I take methocarbamol after drinking to help me sleep?**

It's not a good idea. Taking it at bedtime after drinking means both drugs peak while you're falling asleep, when combined sedation is most dangerous. Wait until the alcohol has cleared (roughly one standard drink per hour on average, though this varies) or skip that dose. Missing one dose of a muscle relaxant is rarely a problem.

**What happens if you mix methocarbamol and alcohol?**

Most often, much stronger drowsiness, dizziness, blurred vision, and unsteadiness than either causes alone, plus a rough next morning. More serious effects, such as fainting, confusion, seizures, slowed breathing, or coma, are more likely with large amounts or when another sedating drug is involved. Call 911 if someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, confused, or having a seizure.

**Why does methocarbamol turn urine dark?**

Methocarbamol can turn urine brown, black, blue, or green. This is a known and harmless effect of the drug. If dark urine comes with yellow skin or eyes, belly pain, or feeling very unwell, though, see a doctor, since those can be signs of a different problem.

**Does DHM make it safe to drink on methocarbamol?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces the interaction between methocarbamol and alcohol, and it does not make the combination safe. Because DHM may act on the brain's GABA system, which many sedating drugs also affect, check with your doctor or pharmacist before combining it with methocarbamol or any other sedating medicine.
